catalog_quote: La fonología suprasegmental, por su parte, no presenta complicaciones en yavitero, ya que se reduce al carácter distintivo del acento de intensidad (mientras que en el baniva, por ejemplo, son significativos tanto el tono, combinado con el acento, como la cantidad vocálica). [...] yavitero no presenta rasgos de lengua tonal, a diferencia, por ejemplo, del baniva, su pariente más cercano en la familia arahuaca. [...] acento distintivo, y donde la longitud vocálica y las variaciones de tono lo acompañan, careciendo de autonomía fonémica. El acento en yavitero cae casi siempre en la primera o la segunda sílaba de la palabra, sin que importe el número total de sílabas que ésta tenga. El poder discriminatorio del acento se comprueba en una serie de pares mínimos, como los que ofrecemos a continuación: wíjla ['wila]: peinar; wijlá [wi'Ja]: flecha de cerbatana. kájate ['kahate]: cazabe, pan; kajáte [ka'hatɛ]: frío. jlíjani ['Jihani]: hijo, cría; jlijáni [Ji'hani]: garrapata pequeña [...] tercera sílaba de la palabra. Tal ocurre, por ejemplo, en las siguientes palabras: wakuláya [waku'laja]: aguaita-caminos (ave); walipópo [wali'popo] [...] préstamos lingüísticos que no llegaron a ser asimilados (o sólo lo fueron en grado incipiente) por el sistema sonoro del yavitero, como los que siguen: terekáyu [tere'kaju]: terecay (tortuga); morokóto [moro'koto]: morocoto (pez) ...
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.translation: Suprasegmental phonology presents no complications in Yavitero, since it reduces to the distinctive character of the intensity (stress) accent (whereas in Baniva, for example, both tone combined with accent and vowel quantity are significant). [...] [a language of] distinctive accent, where vowel length and pitch variation accompany it, lacking phonemic autonomy. The accent in Yavitero falls almost always on the first or the second syllable of the word, regardless of the total number of syllables it has. The discriminatory power of the accent is demonstrated by a series of minimal pairs [...]. (E. E. Mosonyi 2002:133, open PDF: Yavitero 'también presenta un acento fonémico de intensidad, incluso uno solo por palabra' = 'also has a phonemic intensity accent, indeed only one per word'.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (dynamic/intensity accent) is phonemic/contrastive, one primary stress per word, no tone; its position is lexically restricted to a window at the left edge -- almost always the first or second syllable counted from the beginning of the word, irrespective of word length -- with minimal pairs distinguishing the two; a minority of words (e.g. wakuláya, walipópo, wirirí, terekáyu, morokóto) carry it on the third syllable. Morphology interacts: adding a possessive suffix (-ne etc.) moves the accent one syllable to the left unless it is already initial (síja > síjane, mayúlu > máyulune).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; E. E. Mosonyi 2002 says explicitly one intensity accent per word ('incluso uno solo por palabra').
new_statements.exceptions: Third-syllable stress in some words, list beginning 'wakuláya [waku'laja] aguaita-caminos (ave); walipópo [wali'popo] tordo maicero; wirirí [wiri'ri] pato.; terekáyu [tere'kaju] terecay; morokóto [moro'koto]' (several look like regional loan names); leftward accent shift under possessive suffixation unless accent is on the first syllable, 'en cuyo caso permanece invariable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements refer to the (grammatical) word in citation form as produced by the single last speaker; vowel length and pitch are described as non-phonemic concomitants of stress. The chapter text was read only through Google Books snippet scanned (saved feed XML), not a page scan; the open ILLA 3 article by the same first author confirms phonemic intensity stress but gives no position.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Mosonyi sources describe the speech of the last known speaker, Águeda Largo of Yavita (Yavitero dialect proper, Glottolog yavi1245); nothing is said about the historical Pareni variety (pare1276). E. E. Mosonyi 2002 adds that the single intensity accent per word was observed 'en labios de la señora Águeda Largo' and speculates that Yavitero may earlier have had distinctive tonal accents like Baniva de Maroa.
